blocks.text: Blue copper(II) sulphate crystals, white barium sulphate powder and the salt in your soup are all made in the laboratory by three completely different routes. Choosing the wrong route wastes the whole practical, so the first question a chemist asks is always the same: is my salt soluble?

blocks.title: Salt
blocks.text: A salt is the compound formed when all or part of the replaceable hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or by the ammonium ion. Sodium chloride comes from hydrochloric acid, and copper(II) sulphate from tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid.

blocks.markdown:
## Types of salt

- **Normal salt** — every replaceable hydrogen has been replaced. NaCl, Na2SO4, CaCO3
- **Acid salt** — only some of the replaceable hydrogen has been replaced, so the salt can still act as an acid. NaHSO4, NaHCO3, KHCO3. Only acids with a basicity of two or more can form them.
- **Basic salt** — contains the hydroxide ion or oxide ion as well as the acid anion, formed when there is insufficient acid. Pb(OH)Cl, Mg(OH)Cl
- **Double salt** — two simple salts crystallised together in a fixed ratio. Potash alum, KAl(SO4)2.12H2O, and ammonium iron(II) sulphate
- **Complex salt** — contains a complex ion that does not split into simple ions in solution, such as sodium tetrahydroxozincate(II)

rows: All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts
Silver chloride and lead(II) chloride are insoluble
Barium and lead(II) sulphates insoluble; calcium sulphate slightly soluble
Sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates are soluble
Sodium, potassium and ammonium are soluble; calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble
blocks.caption: Solubility rules you must memorise

blocks.markdown:
## Four preparation routes

The route depends on whether the salt is soluble and whether the starting base is soluble.

1. **Soluble salt from an insoluble base, carbonate or oxide** — add the solid in excess to warm dilute acid, stir until no more reacts, filter off the unreacted excess, then evaporate the filtrate to saturation and allow it to crystallise. Used for CuSO4, ZnSO4, FeSO4.
2. **Soluble salt from a soluble base, that is an alkali** — you cannot see when to stop, so use titration. Find the exact volumes by titration with an indicator, then repeat with the same volumes and no indicator, and evaporate. Used for NaCl, KNO3, Na2SO4.
3. **Soluble salt from a metal** — add the metal in excess to dilute acid, but only for metals above hydrogen in the activity series. Used for MgSO4, ZnCl2.
4. **Insoluble salt** — precipitation, also called double decomposition. Mix solutions of two suitable soluble salts, then filter, wash the residue with distilled water and dry it. Used for BaSO4, PbCl2, AgCl, CaCO3.

blocks.title: Preparing crystals of copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI)
blocks.prompt: Describe how you would prepare pure dry crystals of CuSO4.5H2O in the laboratory, starting from copper(II) oxide.

steps.text: Choose the route. Copper(II) sulphate is soluble and copper(II) oxide is an insoluble base, so route 1 applies. Note that copper metal itself cannot be used, because copper lies below hydrogen in the activity series and does not displace hydrogen from dilute acid.
Warm about 50 cm3 of dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid in a beaker, without boiling.
Add copper(II) oxide a little at a time, stirring, until some black solid remains undissolved. The excess guarantees that all the acid has been used up. Equation: CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O.
Filter the mixture. The unreacted copper(II) oxide stays on the filter paper and the blue filtrate is the copper(II) sulphate solution.
Evaporate the filtrate over a water bath until it is saturated, which you test by dipping in a glass rod and seeing crystals form on cooling.
Allow the saturated solution to cool slowly so that large blue crystals of CuSO4.5H2O separate out.
Filter off the crystals and dry them between sheets of filter paper. Do not oven-dry, because heat would drive off the water of crystallisation and leave a white powder.

blocks.answer: Excess copper(II) oxide plus warm dilute acid, filter, evaporate to saturation, cool to crystallise, then dry between filter papers

blocks.title: Precipitating an insoluble salt
blocks.text: To make barium sulphate, mix solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate. BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq). Both starting materials are soluble and the by-product sodium chloride stays in solution, so simply filtering, washing and drying gives the pure white solid.

blocks.title: Justify your choice of method
blocks.text: Marks in this topic are given for the reasoning as much as the procedure. Say why you chose the method: 'the salt is insoluble, so precipitation is used' or 'the base is soluble, so the excess could not be filtered off and titration is required'.

points: A salt is formed when the replaceable hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.
All sodium, potassium, ammonium and nitrate salts are soluble; most carbonates are not.
Insoluble base or carbonate plus acid: add in excess, filter, evaporate and crystallise.
Soluble base plus acid: titrate to find the exact volumes, then repeat without indicator.
Insoluble salts are made by precipitation from two soluble salt solutions.
Dry hydrated crystals between filter papers, never in an oven.
